Continuing on from Example 19, the Court holds that the misrepresentation by Barney was innocent and therefore he is not required to pay damages. Fred commences legal action against Dino Inc. Fred has returned the fossil to Barney for nil consideration and incurred $20,000 legal costs for his actions against both Barney and Dino Inc. He obtains judgment against Dino Inc in negligence and receives $70,000 as damages in December 1995. 310. | | | | --- | --- | | **Relevant asset:** | The underlying asset (the fossil) | | **Acquired:** | July 1994 | | **Cost base:** | $50,000 ($30,000 initial cost plus $20,000 legal costs) | | **Disposed of:** | July 1995 | | **Consideration:** | Nil | | **CGT consequences:** | The disposal of the fossil occurred at the time it was returned to Barney. The reduction of the cost base to nil means that there are no CGT consequences for Fred. The legal expenses incurred in relation to his claim against Barney form part of the cost base of the fossil. There are no CGT consequences in respect of the excess recoupment. | **Example 21** **(Variation of Example 1)** 311\. The State Authority is in some haste to acquire the land and therefore offers Wally an extra $50,000 to expedite the process. The contract for the sale specifies that $180,000 is for the acquisition of the land and the extra $50,000 represents an inducement payment. 312. | | | | --- | --- | | **Relevant asset:** | The right to enter on the land (being the right created and vested in the State Authority) | | **Acquired:** | May 1994 (immediately before disposal) | | **Cost base:** | A proportion of the legal expenses relating to the contract (the balance being attributable to the sale of the land) | | **Disposed of:** | May 1994 | | **Consideration:** | $50,000 | | **CGT consequences:** | Subsection 160M(6) applies to assess the capital gain. Even if subsection 160M(6) did not apply, the capital gain would be assessable under subsection 160M(7); the relevant asset being the notional asset created as a result of the operation of subsection 160M(7). | _**Note:** See Example 1 for the effect of CGT on the other amount._ **Example 22** 313\. XYZ (an accounting firm) is sued by its former client, BCD Ltd, over work done in carrying out a due diligence examination of a company acquired by BCD Ltd in June 1991. The company was acquired for consideration of $19m, which BCD Ltd now believes was excessive. 314\. XYZ and BCD Ltd reach an out of Court settlement in March 1994, under which XYZ pays to BCD Ltd $1 million as compensation for the excess consideration paid to acquire the shares in the company, and in full settlement of all claims that BCD may have against XYZ or any of its principals. XYZ also incurs legal costs of $500,000 in defending the claim and in reaching the settlement. 315\. XYZ has professional indemnity insurance coverage and their insurers agree to meet the full amount of the settlement including all legal costs, after adjusting for a deductible amount of $250,000. Under the terms of this agreement the insurers pay an amount of $750,000 directly to BCD Ltd in June 1994, and the balance of the legal costs ($500,000) to XYZ. At the same time XYZ pays the balance of the agreed settlement amount, $250,000, to BCD Ltd. **_Consequences for BCD Ltd_** 316. | | | | --- | --- | | **Relevant asset:** | The shares acquired in the company | | **Acquired:** | June 1991 | | **Cost base:** | $18 million (adjusted under subsection 160ZH(11)) | | **Disposed of:** | Not applicable. There has been no disposal by BCD Ltd of the shares. | | **Consideration:** | Not applicable | | **CGT consequences:** | There is no disposal of the underlying asset. The cost base of the shares is reduced by the recoupment (being $1 million). | **_Consequences for XYZ_** 317. | | | | --- | --- | | **Relevant Asset:** | The right to seek indemnity from the professional indemnity insurer | | **Acquired:** | When the insurable event occurred (June 1991) | | **Cost Base:** | The amount required to be paid to BCD Ltd plus the legals incurred in defending the claim ($1.5 million). | | **Disposed of:** | At the time of entering into the settlement agreement (June 1994) | | **Consideration:** | $1.25 million | | **CGT consequences:** | A net capital loss of $250,000 may arise. | _**Note:** XYZ may be able to claim the total of the amount to be paid to BCD Ltd and the legals costs as deductible expenditure under subsection 51(1). Further, the compensation received from the insurer may represent assessable income of XYZ under either subsection 25(1) or paragraph 26(j)._ **Example 23** 318\. Jill Jones invites her friend Mary Mills, to her home for dinner. Unfortunately, it is a dark and stormy night, and her friend slips and falls on Jill's front driveway. Mary suffers a broken leg, and on advice from her lawyer brother, decides to end her friendship with Jill and sue her for $10,000. 319\. Jill does not have any insurance and therefore has no right of indemnity for any potential loss. In July 1995, before the matter gets to Court, the parties agree to a settlement under which Jill pays Mary $8,000 in full settlement of her claims. **_Consequences for Mary_** 320\. Mary derives a net capital gain of $8,000 (ignoring any legal costs) which relates wholly to her personal injury and is therefore exempt under subsection 160ZB(1). **_Consequences for Jill_** 321\. Jill has paid an amount of $8,000 to satisfy Mary's claims for compensation. That payment, however, does not relate to the acquisition of any asset by Jill. Accordingly, there is no capital loss in respect of the payment. **Example 24** 322\. On 30 September 1985 X Co entered into an agreement with Y Co to purchase for $3m a development site for the construction of a block of home units. The contract was based on Y Co's representations that the zoning permitted such a development. X Co's solicitor settled the purchase without checking the zoning certificate. When X Co lodged a development application, the zoning certificate showed that there was no such zoning and the site was subject to a restrictive heritage conservation order. By this time, Y Co had been liquidated. X Co sued its solicitor for damages. 323\. X Co provided evidence at the hearing that the land was worth $1m, and would have been worth $4m at the time of entering into the contract had the zoning been as represented. X Co obtained $3.5m in damages from the solicitor, and the solicitor's insurers paid this amount on 30 September 1993. X Co's legals totalled $30,000. The award for damages did not include any additional amount for any potential taxation liability. The land was later sold by X Co on 31 December 1993 for $1m. 324. | | | | --- | --- | | **Relevant asset:** | The land | | **Acquired:** | 30 September 1985 | | **Cost Base:** | Nil (total acquisition cost of $3,030,000 reduced by the recoupment of $3,500,000) | | **Disposed of:** | 30 September 1993 | | **Consideration:** | $3.5 million, applied to the cost base | | **CGT consequences:** | A net capital gain arises on the later disposal of the land for $1m | **Example 25** 325\. Doctor Joseph is a GP with a small local practice which he acquired in 1972. In March 1991, one of Joseph's patients suffers from Joseph's professional negligence, and successfully sues Joseph for malpractice, receiving from Joseph in December 1991 an amount of $100,000. Joseph pays out the agreed settlement sum to his former patient, and seeks recovery of that amount under the terms of his professional indemnity insurance policy. The insurance company pays out $100,000 to Joseph under the policy. **_Consequences for the former patient_** 326. | | | | --- | --- | | **Relevant asset:** | The right to sue for malpractice | | **Acquired:** | March 1991 | | **Cost base:** | Any legal costs connected with the claim. It may also include the costs of taking remedial action (e.g., additional surgery, etc). | | **Disposed of:** | On entering into the settlement agreement with Joseph (December 1991) | | **Consideration:** | $100,000 | | **CGT consequences:** | A net capital gain may arise which is then subject to the exemption under subsection 160ZB(1) | _**Note:** subsection 25(1) may apply to assess any income components._ **_Consequences for Joseph_** 327. | | | | --- | --- | | **Relevant asset:** | The right to seek indemnity under the insurance policy | | **Acquired:** | March 1991 | | **Cost base:** | Any legal costs connected with the claim. It also includes the payment to his former patient. | | **Disposed of:** | On entering into the settlement agreement with his former patient (December 1991) | | **Consideration:** | $100,000 | | **CGT consequences:** | No capital gain or loss arises | _**Note:** there may be consequences under the general income tax provisions for the payment and the insurance recovery._ **Example 26** 328\. Alex is a highly successful security consultant, running a business he commenced in 1982. In 1991, at the age of fifty, he decides to retire and sells his consultancy business to Simon, a colleague and former employee. The contract for sale includes a restrictive covenant, which effectively prohibits Alex from operating or being involved with any form of security operation within 500 km of his former business for a period of five years from the date of the contract. 329\. In March 1993, Alex joins with his son to establish Nightwatch, a security service for the homes, shops and businesses in his local area. Simon successfully sues Alex for his breach of the covenant, and seeks damages on a number of heads of claim (including lost profits and the reduction in value of his goodwill). The Court awards damages of $10,000 for the breach of the covenant, but does not accept that there has been any damage to Simon's goodwill. Simon is also granted an injunction against Alex which effectively restrains his activities for the balance of the covenant term. 330. | | | | --- | --- | | **Relevant asset:** | The right to seek compensation for the breach of the terms of the covenant | | **Acquired:** | March 1993 | | **Cost base:** | Any legal costs connected with the claim | | **Disposed of:** | On judgment by the Court | | **Consideration:** | $10,000 | | **CGT consequences:** | A capital gain or loss may arise. The rights under the covenant continue, and could not be said to be permanently damaged or reduced in value by Alex's breach of the covenant. | **Example 27** 331\. Al is the manager of Chicago Shoe Company's major outlet. In February 1991 Al embezzles $2 million from moneys held in trust by Chicago Shoe Company for another associated company. Chicago Shoe Company discovers the loss and takes immediate action to recover the money. The company takes action against Al, Darcy Financial Services (their financial advisers) and the Polk Insurance Company. As a result of this action Chicago Shoe Company agrees to settle the claims and receives a total of $2.9 million in May 1993 ($1 million from Al, $700,000 from Darcy and $1.2 million from Polk). 332. | | | | --- | --- | | **Relevant asset:** | The right to seek compensation in respect of the theft | | **Acquired:** | February 1991 | | **Cost base:** | $2 million plus legal fees | | **Disposed of:** | On settlement (May 1993) | | **Consideration:** | $2.9 million | | **CGT Consequences:** | Chicago Shoe Company will be assessed on a net capital gain | _**Note:** The loss cannot be claimed as a deduction under either section 71 or subsection 51(1) as it is capital in nature and not an inherent risk of carrying on the business of retail selling._ **Example 28** 333\. Stephen is a junior executive with a company. As his home is in an area not serviced by public transport, he has acquired a car which he uses to travel to and from the office. On Saturday 1 April, Stephen parks his car at the local shopping mall's car park. While Stephen does his shopping, out in the car park Megan misjudges the width of her four wheel drive vehicle (complete with bull bar) and causes significant damage to Stephen's car. The damage requires his car to be off the road for several weeks, during which time Stephen is forced to travel to and from work by taxi. 334\. Stephen takes action against Megan to recover the cost of repairs to his car together with the cost of the taxi travel to and from work to the extent that the cost exceeds his normal cost of travelling. On 25 June his action is successful and he later receives damages, which are clearly defined under separate heads in the award entered in the Court. 335. | | | | --- | --- | | **Relevant asset:** | The right to seek compensation | | **Acquired:** | 1 April | | **Cost base:** | The additional costs of the taxi travel to and from work to the extent that the cost exceeds his normal cost of travelling | | **Disposed of:** | 25 June | | **Consideration:** | That part of the payment which is specified in the award to be in respect of his claim for taxi fares | | **CGT Consequences:** | The amount received for the cost of repairs will have no CGT consequences as the underlying asset (the car) is not an asset for CGT purposes. The amount received as reimbursement for the taxi fares should produce no capital gain or loss (consideration received equals cost base). | _**Note:** Any amount specified in the judgment as received for his inconvenience or personal suffering would be exempt under subsection 160ZB(1)._ **Detailed contents list** 336. | | | | --- | --- | | | para | | What this Ruling is about | 1 | | Class of correctness.justification: All four conclusions match the reference: (a) patent is property (grounded in the legislation itself, Patents Act 1990 s 13(2) 'personal property'); (b) bare know-how is neither property nor a legal/equitable right (TD 2000/33 paras 1-2); (c) the employment contract confers a legal right despite non-assignability; (d) a universal workplace-safety entitlement is not a CGT asset, contrasted with the individual contractual right in (c). The s 108-5(1) test is quoted verbatim. Not 5 because the WHS Act s 267(a) proposition is asserted without its text being captured, so not every claim is borne out by the sources in front of the reader.

completeness.justification: Every reference point is covered, including the contrast between (c) and (d) (individual contractual right vs right enjoyed by all workers) and the non-transferability point in (c); the candidate adds the correct TD 2000/33 para 4 qualification that contract/licence rights in know-how are CGT assets, and the accrued compensation-right distinction in (d). The leading authority, Hepples v FCT, is engaged by name with pinpoints to TR 95/35 paras 39-47 (which quote Gummow, Brennan and Gaudron JJ in the captured text), though the answer itself quotes no passage of the judgment, barring 5.

faithfulness.justification: The governing statutory words of s 108-5(1) are set out verbatim and verified from [[1]] (including Note 1's 'right to enforce a contractual obligation'); the patent claims are verified word-for-word from [[2]] (s 13(1)-(2)); the depreciating-asset aside is verified from [[3]] (s 40-30(2)(c)); the know-how claims are verified from [[4]] (TD 2000/33 paras 1-4); the personal-services and compensation-right claims are verified from [[5]] (paras 33, 34, 39-47 and 153 all in the capture); WHS s 19 is verified from [[6]]. The one unverified claim is WHS Act s 267(a) — the capture is truncated at s 21 — a minor, ancillary proposition on which the (d) conclusion does not rest.

helpfulness.justification: Tightly structured for a professional: governing test stated first with the statutory words set out, each limb given a bolded conclusion with supporting authority, and the right caveats included (unpatented-know-how assumption in (b); enforceable-entitlement carve-out in (d)); no padding and no research narration. It lacks a concrete closing next step (e.g., directing the reader to TD 2000/33 and TR 95/35 paras 39-47, or to check the applicable State WHS statute), which keeps it from 5.

citation_grounding.justification: Every material claim is anchored at the claim to relevant authority, and the statutory propositions rest on the captured words of the legislation itself: s 108-5(1) and Note 1 ([[1]]), Patents Act s 13 ([[2]]), s 40-30(2)(c) ([[3]]), WHS Act s 19 ([[6]]); the ruling/determination pinpoints ([[4]], [[5]]) are verified against extensive captured text. A small minority is unverified: WHS Act s 267(a) is not in the capture (truncated at s 21), and applying s 40-30(2)(c) to a patent assumes the uncaptured s 995-1 definition of 'intellectual property'. No irrelevant or unsupportive citations.

judge_output.summary: Accurate, fully-argued answer matching the reference on all four limbs, densely claim-anchored to largely verified primary sources; the one audit gap is the WHS Act s 267 proposition, whose text was not captured.

completeness.justification: Every key point in the reference is covered: purchase price as first element, all three incidental costs (legal fees, stamp duty, valuation fees) as second element, the $265,660 total, the non-deductibility caveat and the GST-input-tax-credit point. The computation is laid out as a workings table the reader can follow line by line, and no judicial authority is engaged by this straightforward statutory computation.

faithfulness.justification: Every load-bearing claim is anchored at the claim and verified from captured text: first-element rule verified by the full capture of s 110-25(2) [[1]], second-element rule by s 110-25(3) [[1]], legal and valuation fees by s 110-35(2)'s captured words 'remuneration for the services of a surveyor, valuer... or legal adviser' [[2]], and stamp duty by s 110-35(4) 'stamp duty or other similar duty' [[2]]. The only unanchored remark (no GST adjustment needed) is low-importance and is in fact supported by Note 2 to s 110-25(1) in capture [[1]]; the governing statutory words stand set out verbatim in the anchored captures, so a reviewer can audit everything without leaving the page.

helpfulness.justification: The workings table and treatment column are excellent and directly answer the question, but the answer lacks the elements level 3 names: the governing statutory words are not set out in the answer itself, and there is no concrete closing next step (e.g. confirm non-deductibility under s 110-38 or note Div 121 record-keeping) — the closing GST sentence is a premise note, not a next step, so under the ladder the answer falls to level 2 despite being otherwise well pitched.

citation_grounding.justification: Both citations are primary legislation (ITAA 1997 ss 110-25 and 110-35) anchored at the specific claims they support, and the captures contain the full operative text verifying each claim: s 110-25(2)-(3) for the first and second elements, s 110-35(2) for legal/valuation fees and s 110-35(4) for stamp duty. There are no irrelevant, teaser or unverified citations — dense claim-level verified grounding throughout.

judge_output.summary: Correct $265,660 cost base, worked in a clear table with every line anchored at the claim to fully captured primary legislation (ss 110-25(2)-(3), 110-35(2), (4) ITAA 1997); loses marks only for not quoting the operative words in the answer itself and for omitting a closing next step.

Income Tax Assessment Act 1997 **CHAPTER 3** **-** **SPECIALIST LIABILITY RULES** **PART 3-1** **-** **CAPITAL GAINS AND LOSSES: GENERAL TOPICS** ![](https://www.ato.gov.au/law/view/images/plusbox.gif) View history note ![](https://www.ato.gov.au/law/view/images/minusbox.gif) Hide history note History Pt 3-1 inserted by No 46 of 1998. **Division 104** **-** **CGT events** ![](https://www.ato.gov.au/law/view/images/plusbox.gif) View history note ![](https://www.ato.gov.au/law/view/images/minusbox.gif) Hide history note History Div 104 inserted by No 46 of 1998. **Subdivision 104-A** **-** **Disposals** **SECTION 104-10** **Disposal of a CGT asset: CGT event A1** **104-10(1)** **_CGT event A1_** happens if you \* dispose of a \* CGT asset. **104-10(2)** [View history reference](https://www.ato.gov.au/law/view/document?LocID=PAC%2F19970038%2F104-10(2)&db=HISTFT&stylesheet=HIST "View history reference") You **_dispose of_** a \* CGT asset if a change of ownership occurs from you to another entity, whether because of some act or event or by operation of law. However, a change of ownership does not occur if you stop being the legal owner of the asset but continue to be its beneficial owner. ##### Note: A change in the trustee of a trust does not constitute a change in the entity that is the trustee of the trust (see subsection [960-100(2)](https://www.ato.gov.au/law/view/document?LocID=%22PAC%2F19970038%2F960-100(2)%22) ). This means that CGT event A1 will not happen merely because of a change in the trustee. ![](https://www.ato.gov.au/law/view/images/plusbox.gif) View history note ![](https://www.ato.gov.au/law/view/images/minusbox.gif) Hide history note History S 104-10(2) substituted by No 19 of 2010, s 3 and Sch 1 item 16, effective 24 March 2010. S 104-10(2) formerly read: > **104-10(2)** > > You > > **_dispose of_** > a > \* > CGT asset if a change of ownership occurs from you to another entity, whether because of some act or event or by operation of law. However, a change of ownership does not occur: > > > > **(a)** if you stop being the legal owner of the asset but continue to be its beneficial owner; or > > > > **(b)** merely because of a change of trustee. **104-10(3)** The time of the event is: **(a)** when you enter into the contract for the \* disposal; or **(b)** if there is no contract - when the change of ownership occurs. > **Example:** > > In June 1999 you enter into a contract to sell land. The contract is settled in October 1999. You make a capital gain of > $ > 50,000. > > The gain is made in the 1998-99 income year (the year you entered into the contract) and not the 1999-2000 income year (the year that settlement takes place). ##### Note 1: If the contract falls through before completion, this event does not happen because no change in ownership occurs. ##### Note 2: If the asset was compulsorily acquired from you: see subsection (6). **104-10(4)** [View history reference](https://www.ato.gov.au/law/view/document?LocID=PAC%2F19970038%2F104-10(4)&db=HISTFT&stylesheet=HIST "View history reference") You make a **_capital gain_** if the \* capital proceeds from the disposal are _more_ than the asset ' s \* cost base. You make a **_capital loss_** if those capital proceeds are _less_ than the asset ' s \* reduced cost base. **Exceptions** **104-10(5)** [View history reference](https://www.ato.gov.au/law/view/document?LocID=PAC%2F19970038%2F104-10(5)&db=HISTFT&stylesheet=HIST "View history reference") A \* capital gain or \* capital loss you make is disregarded if: **(a)** you \* acquired the asset before 20 September 1985; or **(b)** for a lease that you granted: > **(i)** it was granted before that day; or > **(ii)** if it has been renewed or extended > - > the start of the last renewal or extension occurred before that day. [View history reference](https://www.ato.gov.au/law/view/document?LocID=PAC%2F19970038%2F104-10(5)(b)&db=HISTFT&stylesheet=HIST "View history reference") ##### Note 1: You can make a gain if you dispose of shares in a company, or an interest in a trust, that you acquired before that day: see CGT event K6. ##### Note 2: A capital gain or loss you make because you assign a right under or in relation to a general insurance policy you held with an HIH company to the Commonwealth, the trustee of the HIH Trust or a prescribed entity is also disregarded: see section 322-15. ##### Note 3: A capital gain or loss made by a demerging entity from CGT event A1 happening as a result of a demerger is also disregarded: see section [125-155](https://www.ato.gov.au/law/view/document?LocID=%22PAC%2F19970038%2F125-155%22) . ##### Note 4: A capital gain or loss you make because of section [16AI](https://www.ato.gov.au/law/view/document?LocID=%22PAC%2F19590006%2F16AI%22) of the _Banking Act 1959_ is disregarded: see section [253-10](https://www.ato.gov.au/law/view/document?LocID=%22PAC%2F19970038%2F253-10%22) of this Act. Section [16AI](https://www.ato.gov.au/law/view/document?LocID=%22PAC%2F19590006%2F16AI%22) of the _Banking Act 1959_ : (a) reduces your right to be paid an amount by an ADI in connection with an account to the extent of your entitlement under Division [2AA](https://www.ato.gov.au/law/view/document?LocID=%22PAC%2F19590006%2FPtII-Div2AA%22) of Part [II](https://www.ato.gov.au/law/view/document?LocID=%22PAC%2F19590006%2FPtII%22) of that Act to be paid an amount by APRA; and (b) provides that, to the extent of the reduction, the right becomes a right of APRA. ##### Note 5: A capital gain or loss you make because, under section 62ZZL of the _Insurance Act 1973_ , you dispose of a CGT asset consisting of your rights against a general insurance company to APRA is disregarded: see section [322-30](https://www.ato.gov.au/law/view/document?LocID=%22PAC%2F19970038%2F322-30%22) of this Act. ![](https://www.ato.gov.au/law/view/images/plusbox.gif) View history note ![](https://www.ato.gov.au/law/view/images/minusbox.gif) Hide history note History S 104-10(5) amended by No 42 of 2009, s 3 and Sch 1 item 17, by inserting notes 4 and 5 at the end, effective 23 June 2009. S 104-10(5) amended by No 90 of 2002, No 169 of 2001 and No 173 of 2000. **Compulsory acquisition** **104-10(6)** If the asset was \* acquired from you by an entity under a power of compulsory acquisition conferred by an \* Australian law or a \* foreign law, the time of the event is the earliest of: **(a)** when you received compensation from the entity; or **(b)** when the entity became the asset ' s owner; or **(c)** when the entity entered it under that power; or **(d)** when the entity took possession under that power. ##### Note: You may be able to choose a roll-over if an asset is compulsorily acquired: see Subdivision [124-B](https://www.ato.gov.au/law/view/document?LocID=%22PAC%2F19970038%2FSDiv124-B%22) . **104-10(7)** (Repealed by No 119 of 2013) ![](https://www.ato.gov.au/law/view/images/plusbox.gif) View history note ![](https://www.ato.gov.au/law/view/images/minusbox.gif) Hide history note History S 104-10(7) repealed by No 119 of 2013, s 3 and Sch 1 item 11, applicable: (a) to the extent the amendments affect the _A New Tax System (Wine Equalisation Tax) Act 1999_ - in relation to financial years commencing on or after 30 June 2013; and (b) to the extent the amendments affect Parts [3-1](https://www.ato.gov.au/law/view/document?LocID=%22PAC%2F19970038%2FPt3-1%22) and [3-3](https://www.ato.gov.au/law/view/document?LocID=%22PAC%2F19970038%2FPt3-3%22) of the _Income Tax Assessment Act 1997_ (about capital gains and losses) - in relation to CGT events happening on or after 30 June 2013; and (c) otherwise - in relation to income years commencing on or after 30 June 2013. An entity may choose to have the amendments also apply, in relation to the entity: (a) to the extent the amendments affect Parts [3-1](https://www.ato.gov.au/law/view/document?LocID=%22PAC%2F19970038%2FPt3-1%22) and [3-3](https://www.ato.gov.au/law/view/document?LocID=%22PAC%2F19970038%2FPt3-3%22) of the _Income Tax Assessment Act 1997_ - in relation to CGT events happening during the 2008-09 income year and later income years; and (b) other than to the extent the amendments affect those Parts or the _A New Tax System (Wine Equalisation Tax) Act 1999_ - in relation to the 2008-09 income year and later income years. It does _not_ include indexation of those elements. ##### Note: The reduced cost base is reduced by net input tax credits: see section [103-30](https://www.ato.gov.au/law/view/document?LocID=%22PAC%2F19970038%2F103-30%22) . ![](https://www.ato.gov.au/law/view/images/plusbox.gif) View history note ![](https://www.ato.gov.au/law/view/images/minusbox.gif) Hide history note History S 110-55(1) amended by No 95 of 2004. **5 elements of the reduced cost base** **110-55(2)** All of the elements (except the third one) of the **_reduced cost base_** of a \* CGT asset are the same as those for the \* cost base. **110-55(3)** The third element is: **(a)** [View history reference](https://www.ato.gov.au/law/view/document?LocID=PAC%2F19970038%2F110-55(3)(a)&db=HISTFT&stylesheet=HIST "View history reference") any amounts worked out under whichever of the following subparagraphs applies: > **(i)** if Division > [58](https://www.ato.gov.au/law/view/document?LocID=%22PAC%2F19970038%2FDiv58%22) > does not apply to the asset > - > any amount included in your assessable income for any income year because of a balancing adjustment for the asset; and **(b)** [View history reference](https://www.ato.gov.au/law/view/document?LocID=PAC%2F19970038%2F110-55(3)(b)&db=HISTFT&stylesheet=HIST "View history reference") any amount that would have been so included apart from any of these (which provide relief from including a balancing charge in your assessable income): > **(i)** section > [40-365](https://www.ato.gov.au/law/view/document?LocID=%22PAC%2F19970038%2F40-365%22) > ; or > **(ii)** any of these former sections > - > section > [42-285](https://www.ato.gov.au/law/view/document?LocID=%22PAC%2F19970038%2F42-285%22&db=HISTFT&Caller=PAC%2F19970038%2F110-55) > , > [42-290](https://www.ato.gov.au/law/view/document?LocID=%22PAC%2F19970038%2F42-290%22&db=HISTFT&Caller=PAC%2F19970038%2F110-55) > or > [42-293](https://www.ato.gov.au/law/view/document?LocID=%22PAC%2F19970038%2F42-293%22&db=HISTFT&Caller=PAC%2F19970038%2F110-55) > ; S 110-55(3) amended by No 77 of 2001, No 164 of 1999 and No 93 of 1999. **What does not form part of the reduced cost base** **110-55(4)** The **_reduced cost base_** does not include an amount to the extent that you have deducted or can deduct it (including because of a balancing adjustment) or could have deducted apart from paragraph [43-70(2)(h)](https://www.ato.gov.au/law/view/document?LocID=%22PAC%2F19970038%2F43-70(2)%22) . ##### Note: That paragraph excludes from deductibility under Division [43](https://www.ato.gov.au/law/view/document?LocID=%22PAC%2F19970038%2FDiv43%22) expenditure that qualifies for the heritage conservation rebate. **110-55(5)** [View history reference](https://www.ato.gov.au/law/view/document?LocID=PAC%2F19970038%2F110-55(5)&db=HISTFT&stylesheet=HIST "View history reference") The **_reduced cost base_** does not include an amount that you could have deducted for a \* CGT asset had you used it wholly for the \* purpose of producing assessable income. ![](https://www.ato.gov.au/law/view/images/plusbox.gif) View history note ![](https://www.ato.gov.au/law/view/images/minusbox.gif) Hide history note History S 110-55(5) substituted by No 77 of 2001 and amended by No 93 of 1999. **110-55(6)** Expenditure does _not_ form part of the **_reduced cost base_** to the extent of any amounts you have received as \* recoupment of it. correctness.justification: The conclusion matches the reference exactly: indexed cost base $56,900 (50,000 × 68.7/60.6 = 1.134, plus unindexed $200 brokerage), no gain under s 104-10(4), and no loss because the unindexed reduced cost base of $50,200 is below the $55,000 proceeds. Rules are stated from the legislation itself (ss 114-1, 110-35(2), 104-10(4), 110-55(1)-(2)) and every figure is borne out by the captures; only the rubric's requirement that operative words be quoted, plus the trivial 'more than 12 months' phrasing of the s 114-10 'at least 12 months' condition, keeps it from 5.

completeness.justification: All the reference's substantive steps are present: eligibility and freeze, CPI figures, factor computation, exclusion of post-September 1999 brokerage from indexation, the gain test against the indexed cost base, and the loss test against the unindexed reduced cost base. Minor omissions: the disposal is not expressly labelled CGT event A1 (only s 104-10(4) is cited) and the s 960-275 indexation formula/rounding mechanic is not articulated; no judicial authority is relevant to this computation.

faithfulness.justification: Roughly 85-90% of load-bearing claims are anchored at the claim and verified from captured text; the residue — the 12-month holding condition (no s 114-10 citation) and the rounding of the factor to three decimal places (no s 960-275 citation) — floats free. The governing statutory words are paraphrased in the answer rather than set out verbatim, which the upper levels require.

helpfulness.justification: Tightly structured and correctly pitched: workings table for the indexed cost base, separate gain and loss tests, and a clear result for 2022-23 with no padding. It lacks the closing next step a partner would want (e.g. noting the discount method would instead produce a $2,400 assessable gain, so indexation should be chosen, and pointing to s 960-275) and paraphrases rather than sets out the governing words, so it falls just short of level 5.

citation_grounding.justification: All five citations are anchored at their claims and verified from captured text: s 114-1 (eligibility and the 30 September 1999 freeze, via the former text and Note 2/Note 5), the ATO CPI table (60.6 for March 1993, 68.7 for September 1999 — appropriate administrative grounding for index numbers), s 110-35(2) ('broker' remuneration), s 104-10(4) (gain/loss tests) and s 110-55(1) (reduced cost base 'does not include indexation'). Only the s 960-275 rounding mechanic and the 12-month condition rest on no citation, a small minority of unverified material claims.

judge_output.summary: Correct nil-gain/nil-loss conclusion with claim-anchored, captured primary-source grounding for every operative rule; held back from top marks by the absence of verbatim statutory quotation, the uncited s 960-275 rounding mechanic and s 114-10 12-month condition, and no closing next step.

(2) You dispose of a \\* CGT asset if a change of [ownership](https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#owner) occurs from you to another entity, whether because of some act or event or by operation of law. However, a change of [ownership](https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#owner) does not occur if you stop being the legal [owner](https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#owner) of the asset but continue to be its beneficial [owner](https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#owner). Note: A change in the [trustee](https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#trustee) of a trust does not constitute a change in the entity that is the [trustee](https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#trustee) of the trust (see [subsection](https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s87.40.html#subsection)960 - 100(2)). This means that CGT event A1 [will](https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s28.5.html#will) not happen merely because of a change in the [trustee](https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#trustee). (3) The time of the event is: (a) when you enter into the contract for the \\* disposal; or (b) if there is no contract--when the change of [ownership](https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#owner) occurs. Example: In June 1999 you enter into a contract to sell land. The contract is settled in October 1999. You [make](https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#make) a capital gain of $50,000. The gain is made in the 1998 \- 99 [income year](https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#income_year) (the year you entered into the contract) and not the 1999 \- 2000 [income year](https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#income_year) (the year that settlement takes place). Note 1: If the contract falls through before completion, this event does not happen because no change in [ownership](https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#owner) occurs. Note 2: If the asset was compulsorily acquired from you: see [subsection](https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s87.40.html#subsection)(6). (4) You [make](https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#make) a capital gain if the \\* capital proceeds from the disposal are more than the asset's \\* cost base. You [make](https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#make) a capital loss if those capital proceeds are less than the asset's \\* [reduced cost base](https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#reduced_cost_base). Exceptions (5) A \\* capital gain or \\* capital loss you [make](https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#make) is disregarded if: (a) you \\* acquired the asset before 20 September 1985; or (b) for a lease that you granted: (i) it was granted before that day; or (ii) if it has been renewed or extended--the start of the last renewal or extension occurred before that day. Note 1: You can [make](https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#make) a gain if you dispose of [shares](https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#share) in a company, or an interest in a trust, that you acquired before that day: see CGT event K6. Note 2: A capital gain or loss you [make](https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#make) because you assign a right [under](https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#under) or in relation to a [general insurance policy](https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#general_insurance_policy) you [held](https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#held) with an [HIH company](https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#hih_company) to the Commonwealth, the [trustee](https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#trustee) of the [HIH Trust](https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#hih_trust) or a prescribed entity is also disregarded: see section 322 \- 15\. SECT 118.170 Spouse having different main residence ### INCOME TAX ASSESSMENT ACT 1997 - SECT 118.170 **Spouse having different main residence** (1) If, during a period, a \\* dwelling is your main residence and another \\* dwelling is the main residence of your \\* [spouse](https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#spouse) (except a [spouse](https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#spouse) living permanently separately and apart from you), you and your [spouse](https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#spouse) must either: (a) choose one of the dwellings as the main residence of both of you for the period; or (b) nominate the different dwellings as your main residences for the period. (2) If you nominate the different \\* dwellings as your main residences for the period, you split the exemption in accordance with [subsections](https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s152.220.html#subsection)(3) and (4). (3) If your interest in the \\* dwelling you chose was not, during the period, more than half of the total interests in the dwelling, the dwelling is taken to have been your main residence during the period. Otherwise, the dwelling is taken to have been your main residence for half of the period. (4) If your \\* [spouse](https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#spouse)'s interest in the \\* dwelling your [spouse](https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#spouse) chose was not , during the period, more than half of the total interests in the dwelling, the dwelling is taken to have been your [spouse](https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#spouse)'s main residence during the period. Otherwise, the dwelling is taken to have been your [spouse](https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#spouse)'s main residence for half of the period. Example: You and your [spouse](https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#spouse) (who are Australian residents) own a town house as tenants in common in equal [shares](https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#share). You and your [spouse](https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#spouse) also own a beach house as tenants in common, with your interest being 30% and your [spouse](https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#spouse)'s 70%. From 1 July 1999, you live mainly in the town house and your [spouse](https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#spouse) lives mainly in the beach house. On 1 July 2000 you and your [spouse](https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#spouse) dispose of both dwellings. For the period 1 July 1999 \- 30 June 2000 you nominate the town house as your main residence and your [spouse](https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#spouse) nominates the beach house. The town house is taken to be your main residence during the period. The beach house is taken to be your [spouse](https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#spouse)'s main residence during half the period. #### Navigate - [Having a different home from your dependent child](https://www.ato.gov.au/individuals-and-families/investments-and-assets/capital-gains-tax/property-and-capital-gains-tax/your-main-residence-home/living-separately-to-your-spouse-or-children#ato-Havingadifferenthomefromyourdependentchild) - [Having a different home from your spouse](https://www.ato.gov.au/individuals-and-families/investments-and-assets/capital-gains-tax/property-and-capital-gains-tax/your-main-residence-home/living-separately-to-your-spouse-or-children#ato-Havingadifferenthomefromyourspouse) - [Definition of spouse](https://www.ato.gov.au/individuals-and-families/investments-and-assets/capital-gains-tax/property-and-capital-gains-tax/your-main-residence-home/living-separately-to-your-spouse-or-children#ato-Definitionofspouse) ## Having a different home from your dependent child If you and a dependent child under 18 years of age have different homes for a period, for capital gains tax (CGT) purposes you must choose one of the homes as the main residence for both of you for the period. ## Having a different home from your spouse If you and your spouse have different homes for a period, for CGT purposes you and your spouse must either: - choose one of the homes as the main residence for both of you for the period - each nominate one of the different homes as your main residence for the period. If you nominate different homes for the period and you own 50% or less of the home you have nominated, you qualify for an exemption for your share. If you own more than 50%, your share is exempt for half the period you and your spouse have different homes. The same rule applies to your spouse. This rule applies to each main residence the spouses nominate, whether they have sole ownership or own the home jointly (either as joint tenants or tenants in common). ### Example 1: spouses with different main residences On 1 July 1999 Kathy and her spouse Grahame entered into a contract to purchase a townhouse which they lived in together. Grahame owned 70% of the townhouse and Kathy owned the other 30%. On 1 August 2002 they entered into a contract to purchase a beach house, which they owned in equal shares. From 1 May 2003: - Kathy lived in their beach house and nominated it as her main residence. - Grahame kept living in the townhouse and nominated it as his main residence. On 15 April 2026 Kathy and Grahame entered into a contract for the sale of both the townhouse and beach house. **Beach house** As the beach house was Kathy's main residence and she owned 50% of it, she disregards her share of any capital gain or loss for the period she and Grahame had different homes (1 May 2003 to 15 April 2026). As Grahame didn't live in the beach house or nominate it as his main residence when he and Kathy had different homes, he includes his share (50%) of any capital gain or loss for any of the period he owned it. **Townhouse** The total capital gain on the sale of the townhouse was $100,000. Grahame's share of the capital gain is $70,000 (reflecting his 70% ownership interest). Because Grahame owned more than 50% of the townhouse, it is taken to have been his main residence for half of the period when he and Kathy had different homes. He is entitled to the main residence exemption for the entire period that he and Kathy lived together in the townhouse. The amount of the gain that Grahame disregards under the main residence exemption is: - his share of capital gain - multiplied by: days the spouses have one main residence (1 July 1999 to 30 April 2003) - divided by: total days the property was owned (1 July 1999 to 15 April 2026) - equals: amount of gain disregarded for the period that spouses have one main residence. That is: $70,000 × (1400 ÷ 9,786 days) = $10,014 _plus_ - his share of capital gain - multiplied by: 50% - multiplied by: days the spouses have separate main residences (1 May 2003 to 15 April 2026) - divided by: total days the property was owned (1 July 1999 to 15 April 2026) - equals: amount of gain disregarded for the period that spouses have separate main residences. That is: $70,000 × 50% × (8386 days ÷ 9,786 days) = $29,993 The total amount disregarded by Grahame is: $10,014 + $29,993 = $40,007 Grahame's capital gain on the townhouse is therefore: $70,000 − $40,007 = $29,993 Kathy's share of the $100,000 capital gain on the townhouse is $30,000, reflecting her 30% ownership interest. She is entitled to the main residence exemption for the period that she and Grahame lived together in the townhouse. The amount she disregards is: - her share of capital gain - multiplied by: days the spouses have one main residence (1 July 1999 to 30 April 2003) - divided by: total days the property was owned (1 July 1999 to 15 April 2026) - equals: amount of gain disregarded for the period that spouses have one main residence. That is: $30,000 × (1,400 days ÷ 9,786 days) = $4,292 Kathy's capital gain on the townhouse is therefore: $30,000 − $4,292 = $25,708 **CGT discount** Kathy and Grahame can use the CGT discount to reduce their respective capital gains (after applying any capital losses) because they owned the townhouse and beach house for at least 12 months and are Australian residents. For the townhouse, which was bought before 21 September 1999, they have the option of indexing the cost base instead of using the discount. End of example This rule also applies if you choose to [treat a property as your main residence after you move out](https://www.ato.gov.au/individuals-and-families/investments-and-assets/capital-gains-tax/property-and-capital-gains-tax/your-main-residence-home/treating-former-home-as-main-residence), and this choice results in you having a different main residence from your spouse or a dependent child for a period. ### Example 2: different main residences and continuing main residence On 5 February 2000 Anna and her spouse Mark bought a townhouse and moved in together. Anna owned more than 50% of the townhouse. Before moving into the townhouse Anna had lived alone in her own flat. After moving into the townhouse she rented out her flat. On 11 March 2001 Anna sold her flat. She chose to treat the flat as her main residence from 5 February 2000 until she sold it, under the 'continuing main residence status after moving out' rule. On 29 April 2026 Anna and Mark sold their townhouse. Because of Anna's choice, Mark had a different main residence from Anna for the period 5 February 2000 to 11 March 2001. Therefore, Mark must either: - treat Anna's flat as his main residence for that period, or - nominate the townhouse as his main residence for that period. If he chooses to treat Anna's flat as his main residence, a part of any capital gain Mark makes when he sells the townhouse will be taxable. He will not get an exemption for the townhouse for the period that he nominated Anna's flat as his main residence (that is, 5 February 2000 to 11 March 2001). If Mark nominates the townhouse as his main residence, he qualifies for a full exemption on any capital gain he makes when it is sold because he owns 50% or less of it. However, because Mark and Anna had different main residences as a result of Mark's choice, and Anna owned more than 50% of the flat, her gain on the flat will only qualify for a 50% exemption for the period from 5 February 2000 to 11 March 2001. Anna's capital gain on the townhouse for the period 5 February 2000 to 11 March 2001 is taxable. End of example ## Definition of spouse Your spouse is another person who is: - legally married to you - in a relationship with you, and the relationship is registered under a prescribed state or territory law - not legally married to you but lives with you on a genuine domestic basis in a relationship as a couple. SECT 118.185 Partial exemption where dwelling was your main residence during part only of ownership period ### INCOME TAX ASSESSMENT ACT 1997 - SECT 118.185 **Partial exemption where dwelling was your main residence during part only of ownership period** (1) You get only a [partial](https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#part) exemption for a \\* CGT event that happens in relation to a \\* dwelling or your \\* [ownership interest](https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#ownership_interest) in it if: (a) you are an [individual](https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#individual); and (b) the dwelling was your main residence for [part](https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#part) only of your \* [ownership period](https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#ownership_period); and (c) the interest did not \\* pass to you as a beneficiary in, and you did not \\* acquire it as a [trustee](https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#trustee) of, the estate of a deceased [person](https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#person). (2) You calculate your \\* capital gain or \\* capital loss using the [formula](https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s152.125.html#formula): ![Start formula CG or CL amount times start fraction Non-main residence days over Days in your *ownership period end fraction end formula](https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/images/C2004A05138_image.118.png) where: "CG or CL amount" is the \\* capital gain or \\* capital loss you would have made from the \\* CGT event apart from this Subdivision. "non-main residence days" is the number of days in your \\* [ownership period](https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#ownership_period) when the \\* dwelling was not your main residence. Note: The capital gain or loss may be further adjusted if the dwelling was used to produce assessable income: see section 118 \- 190\. Example: You bought a house in July 2020 and moved in immediately. In July 2023, you moved out and began to rent it. You sold it in July 2030, making (apart from this Subdivision) a capital gain of $10,000. At the time you sold the house, you were an Australian resident. You choose to continue to treat the dwelling as your main residence [under](https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#under) section 118 \- 145 (about absences) for the first 6 of the 7 years during which you rented the house out. [Under](https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#under) this section, you will be taken to have made a capital gain of: ![Start formula $10,000 times start fraction 365 over 3,650 end fraction equals $1,000 end formula](https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/images/C2004A05138_image.119.png) (3) However, this section does not apply if, at the time the \* CGT event happens, you: (a) are an \\* excluded foreign resident; or (b) are a foreign resident who does not satisfy the \* [life events test](https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#life_events_test). #### Navigate - helpfulness.justification: Working elements are present: the governing rule is set out (as close paraphrase), the application is laid out in a clear workings table, the arithmetic is shown (70% × ½ = 35%), and the closing section gives the s 118-185 computation and identifies the data needed to produce figures — a usable next step.     extract (page read): [Skip to main content](https://www.ato.gov.au/individuals-and-families/investments-and-assets/capital-gains-tax/property-and-capital-gains-tax/your-main-residence-home/using-your-home-for-rental-or-business#content) [Skip To search](https://www.ato.gov.au/individuals-and-families/investments-and-assets/capital-gains-tax/property-and-capital-gains-tax/your-main-residence-home/using-your-home-for-rental-or-business#search-box) [Skip To Alex Virtual Assistant](https://www.ato.gov.au/individuals-and-families/investments-and-assets/capital-gains-tax/property-and-capital-gains-tax/your-main-residence-home/using-your-home-for-rental-or-business#alex-virtual-assistant) # Using your home for rental or business Check if your CGT main residence exemption is affected if you earn assessable income from your home. **Last updated** 22 June 2026 Print or Download ## On this page - [How it works](https://www.ato.gov.au/individuals-and-families/investments-and-assets/capital-gains-tax/property-and-capital-gains-tax/your-main-residence-home/using-your-home-for-rental-or-business#ato-Howitworks) - [Check if CGT applies](https://www.ato.gov.au/individuals-and-families/investments-and-assets/capital-gains-tax/property-and-capital-gains-tax/your-main-residence-home/using-your-home-for-rental-or-business#ato-CheckifCGTapplies) - [Work out your capital gain or loss](https://www.ato.gov.au/individuals-and-families/investments-and-assets/capital-gains-tax/property-and-capital-gains-tax/your-main-residence-home/using-your-home-for-rental-or-business#ato-Workoutyourcapitalgainorloss) - [Value of home when first used to produce income](https://www.ato.gov.au/individuals-and-families/investments-and-assets/capital-gains-tax/property-and-capital-gains-tax/your-main-residence-home/using-your-home-for-rental-or-business#ato-Valueofhomewhenfirstusedtoproduceincome) - [Rental property becomes your main residence](https://www.ato.gov.au/individuals-and-families/investments-and-assets/capital-gains-tax/property-and-capital-gains-tax/your-main-residence-home/using-your-home-for-rental-or-business#ato-Rentalpropertybecomesyourmainresidence) ## How it works [Your main residence](https://www.ato.gov.au/individuals-and-families/investments-and-assets/capital-gains-tax/property-and-capital-gains-tax/your-main-residence-home/eligibility-for-main-residence-exemption) (your home) is exempt from capital gains tax (CGT) if you are an Australian resident. You’re not entitled to the full main residence exemption from CGT if you rent out part of your home or run a business from home. However, you may be entitled to a partial main residence exemption. When you sell your home, the part you used to earn assessable income (as a rental or to run a business) is subject to CGT. You can usually claim income tax deductions for the part of your home used to produce assessable income. To work out your capital gain or loss, you consider: - the floor area used as a rental or to run a business, including through the [sharing economy](https://www.ato.gov.au/businesses-and-organisations/income-deductions-and-concessions/sharing-economy-and-tax/renting-out-all-or-part-of-your-home) - the period you used it for this purpose - if you [first started using your home for rental or business](https://www.ato.gov.au/individuals-and-families/investments-and-assets/capital-gains-tax/property-and-capital-gains-tax/your-main-residence-home/using-your-home-for-rental-or-business#Valueofhomewhenfirstusedtoproduceincome) after 20 August 1996. If you're a foreign resident when a [CGT event](https://www.ato.gov.au/individuals-and-families/investments-and-assets/capital-gains-tax/cgt-events) happens to your residential property in Australia (for example, you sell it), generally you aren't entitled to claim the main residence exemption. For more information, see [Main residence exemption for foreign residents](https://www.ato.gov.au/individuals-and-families/investments-and-assets/capital-gains-tax/foreign-residents-and-capital-gains-tax/main-residence-exemption-for-foreign-residents). ## Check if CGT applies To work out if CGT applies, you need to determine if you would be allowed a deduction for your home loan interest if you had borrowed money to acquire your home. This is the ‘interest deductibility test’. The interest deductibility test must be applied even if you haven't borrowed money to acquire your home. If you are or would be eligible to claim part of the interest expense, your home is subject to CGT to the same extent. If you have a home loan, you can’t: - reduce the capital gain by not claiming a deduction for some or all of the interest - increase the cost base of your home by the amount of interest you choose not to claim as a deduction. You can still get a full main residence exemption if someone else uses part of your home to produce assessable income and you don't receive assessable income from that person for the use of the property. To help work out if you need to consider CGT, check the scenarios in [Capital gains tax and the main residence exemption](https://www.ato.gov.au/tax-and-super-professionals/for-tax-professionals/prepare-and-lodge/tax-time/tax-time-toolkits/tax-time-toolkit-for-investors/capital-gains-tax-and-the-main-residence-exemption). ### Renting out part of your home If you rent out part of your home for a period: - You can claim a deduction for the home loan interest related to the portion of your home that is rented out. - The capital gain (or loss) for that portion of your home during the rental period would be assessable – for example, the floor area used by tenants. ### Running a business from home You're running a business from home if it’s your principal place of business and you have space set aside just for this purpose. Merely working from home occasionally or by choice doesn’t qualify. You're only eligible for the full main residence exemption if you’re not entitled to claim a deduction for interest expenses. You’re entitled to claim a deduction for part of any home loan interest if: - part of your home is set aside exclusively as a place of business and is clearly identifiable as such - that part of the home isn’t readily adaptable for private use – for example, a doctor's surgery located in a doctor's home. You’re **not** entitled to claim a deduction for interest expenses if you: - use a home study to do work usually done at your place of work - do paid child-minding at home (unless part of your home is set aside exclusively for that purpose). If you’re not entitled to a full main residence exemption because you use your home for business purposes, you may be able to apply the [small business CGT concessions](https://www.ato.gov.au/businesses-and-organisations/income-deductions-and-concessions/incentives-and-concessions/small-business-cgt-concessions) to reduce your capital gain. ## Work out your capital gain or loss You can use the [CGT property exemption tool](https://www.ato.gov.au/calculators-and-tools/capital-gains-tax-property-exemption-tool) to calculate the portion of your home that is subject to CGT. Alternatively, you can work out the assessable part of your capital gain or loss as follows: **Step 1:** Work out the capital gain or loss on your home based on its value when you first used it to produce assessable income. There are exceptions if you first used your home to produce assessable income before 21 August 1996 or inherited your home. For more information see [Value of home when first used to produce income](https://www.ato.gov.au/individuals-and-families/investments-and-assets/capital-gains-tax/property-and-capital-gains-tax/your-main-residence-home/using-your-home-for-rental-or-business#Valueofhomewhenfirstusedtoproduceincome). **Step 2:** Determine the portion of your home's floor area that you set aside to produce assessable income. **Step 3:** Multiply steps 1 and 2. If you: - used your home to produce assessable income right up to when you sold it, this is your assessable capital gain or loss – you don’t need to continue - stopped using your home to produce assessable income before you sold it – continue to step 4. **Step 4:** Determine the number of days you used your home to produce assessable income. **Step 5:** Determine the number of days from the date you first used your home to produce assessable income until you sold it. **Step 6:** Your net capital gain is step 3 × (step 4 ÷ step 5). ### Example: part of home rented throughout ownership period Thomas bought a house on 1 July 2003 for $300,000. He sold it on 30 June 2026 for $700,000. The house was his main residence for the entire time. Throughout the period Thomas owned the house a tenant rented one bedroom, which represented 20% of the house. Both Thomas and the tenant used the living room, bathroom, laundry and kitchen, which represented 30% of the house. Only Thomas used the remainder of the house. This means Thomas is entitled to a 35% deduction (20% + \[30% × 50%\]) for home loan interest (if he incurred it). Using [steps 1 to 6](https://www.ato.gov.au/individuals-and-families/investments-and-assets/capital-gains-tax/property-and-capital-gains-tax/your-main-residence-home/using-your-home-for-rental-or-business#Workouttheassessablepartofyourcapitalgai) Thomas works out his net capital gain as follows. 1. Thomas used his home to produce assessable income from the time he acquired it. Therefore, he uses its initial value to work out his capital gain: $700,000 − $300,000 = $400,000. 2. The portion of the floor area set aside for rental is 35%. 3. Thomas' net capital gain is $400,000 × 35% = $140,000. As he used his home to earn assessable income right up to when he sold it, he doesn’t need to apportion his net capital gain for any period it wasn’t used to produce assessable income. As Thomas owned his house for at least 12 months he can use the CGT discount (50% for individuals) to reduce his capital gain. Thomas's net capital gain would be $70,000. End of example ### Example: part of home used for business for part of ownership period Fatima bought a house in December 1997 for $200,000. It was her main residence. - On 1 November 2018 she started to use 40% of the house for a consultancy business. At that time the market value of the house was $520,000. - On 1 August 2022 she shifted her consultancy practice to separate business premises and used her home solely for private purposes. - On 1 May 2026 she sold her house for $620,000. Using the [steps 1 to 6](https://www.ato.gov.au/individuals-and-families/investments-and-assets/capital-gains-tax/property-and-capital-gains-tax/your-main-residence-home/using-your-home-for-rental-or-business#Workouttheassessablepartofyourcapitalgai), Fatima works out her net capital gain as follows: 1. Her capital gain based on the value of her home when she first used it to produce assessable income is $620,000 − $520,000 = $100,000. 2. The portion of her home's floor area set aside for business was 40%. 3. $100,000 × 40% = $40,000. As Fatima stopped using her home for business before she sold it, she continues to step 4. 4. Fatima used her home to produce assessable income from 1 November 2018 to 1 August 2022, a total of 1,370 days. 5. The period from when she first used her home to produce assessable income until she sold it is 2,739 days (1 November 2018 to 1 May 2026). 6. Fatima's net capital gain is $40,000 × (1,370 ÷ 2,739) = $20,007. For CGT purposes, Fatima is treated as if she acquired the house on 1 November 2018. This is more than 12 months before she sold it, so she can use the CGT discount (50% for individuals) to reduce her capital gain. Fatima's net capital gain would be $10,003. End of example ## Value of home when first used to produce income If you use your home to produce assessable income you are generally taken to have acquired it at the time you first used it for this purpose. This means when you sell your home, you need to use the 'home first used to produce income rule'. You do this by working out the capital gain or loss using its market value at the time you first used it to produce assessable income. If you sell your home within 12 months of when you first use it to produce assessable income, you can’t use the [CGT discount](https://www.ato.gov.au/individuals-and-families/investments-and-assets/capital-gains-tax/cgt-discount#ato-12monthownershiprequirement). ### Market valuation You must get a [market valuation](https://www.ato.gov.au/individuals-and-families/investments-and-assets/capital-gains-tax/market-valuation-of-assets) of your home when you first start using it for rental or business, if this was after 20 August 1996. You need to know this value to calculate your capital gain or loss when you sell it. ### Exclusions to the 'home first used to produce income rule' The 'home first used to produce income rule' doesn't apply if you: - use your home to produce assessable income from the time you acquire it, the rule doesn’t affect you – for an example, see [Rental property becomes your main residence](https://www.ato.gov.au/individuals-and-families/investments-and-assets/capital-gains-tax/property-and-capital-gains-tax/your-main-residence-home/using-your-home-for-rental-or-business#Rentalpropertybecomesyourmainreside) - [inherit a dwelling](https://www.ato.gov.au/individuals-and-families/investments-and-assets/capital-gains-tax/inherited-assets-and-capital-gains-tax/inherited-property-and-cgt) that was a deceased’s main residence – the rule doesn’t apply when you sell the dwelling within 2 years - choose to [continue treating a property as your main residence after you move out](https://www.ato.gov.au/individuals-and-families/investments-and-assets/capital-gains-tax/property-and-capital-gains-tax/your-main-residence-home/treating-former-home-as-main-residence) – when the property is fully exempt, the rule doesn’t apply - don't meet the criteria for a partial main residence exemption, – for example, you either - were a foreign resident when you sold the property - claimed the exemption for another property for the period you lived there. #### Example: 'home first used to produce income rule' doesn't apply Peter bought a house on 1 October 2013 for $550,000. He rented it out until 30 June 2016. Peter moved into the house on 1 July 2016 and lived in it for the entire period until it was sold on 30 March 2026 for $780,000. The ‘home first used to produce income rule’ doesn’t apply as the house was rented from the time Peter bought it. This means that Peter isn’t required to use the market value of the house at the time it was first used to produce assessable income. Peter works out the capital gain based on the cost base of $550,000. Peter is entitled to the main residence exemption from 1 July 2016 to 30 March 2026 (3,560 days). The assessable part of Peter’s capital gain will be calculated as follows: 1. Capital gain for the entire period is $780,000 − $550,000 = $230,000 2. Peter’s home was rented out for 1,004 days (1 October 2013 to 30 June 2016) 3. Peter’s total period of ownership was 4,564 days. 4. Capital gain for the period that was rented out is $230,000 × (1,004 ÷ 4,564) = $50,595. Peter is entitled to the CGT discount of 50% which will reduce his capital gain. Peter’s net capital gain would be $25,297. End of example ### When the rule applies Apart from these exclusions, the rule applies if all the following are true: - you acquired the property on or after 20 September 1985 - you first used the property to produce assessable income after 20 August 1996 - when you sell the property (or another [CGT event](https://www.ato.gov.au/individuals-and-families/investments-and-assets/capital-gains-tax/cgt-events) happens to it), you would be entitled to a partial CGT exemption because you used it to produce assessable income during the time you owned it - you would have been entitled to a full exemption if the sale or other CGT event happened to the property immediately before you first used it to produce assessable income. #### Example: home becomes a rental property Erin bought a house 25 July 2014 for $450,000. The house was her main residence until she moved into a new house on 1 August 2025. On 2 August 2025 she began renting out the old house. At that time, the market value of the old house was $650,000. Erin didn’t want to treat the old house as her main residence under the ‘continuing main residence status after moving out’ option. She wanted the new house to be treated as her main residence from the date she moved into it. On 10 June 2026 Erin sold the old house for $696,000. As Erin is deemed to have acquired the old house for $650,000 on 2 August 2025, she calculates her capital gain to be $46,000. She can’t use the CGT discount to reduce her capital gain as she is taken to have owned it for less than 12 months. End of example Viostream media embed ![](https://image.viostream.com/sls2/16-9/300/media/M2RhMjhkMTktNTc5Mi00Mzk3LWIxNTgtYTQ3NDAwOTBhOGQ4Lzc5MTEyMTYwLWFjZmYtNDFkNS04MGNjLTc5ZjExNjZhZWEwYy83ZDMxYWYxOS1hOGQ5LTRjZjctYjU0ZC1hNGJjMDExMTVmMTQuanBn/selling-a-rental-property-that-was-your-home.jpg) Video Player is loading. For the period the property was rented out, you will be liable for CGT when you sell the property. Use the following formula to work out your CGT when you sell your property: Capital gain or loss × (number of days the property was used to produce assessable income ÷ total number of days you owned the property) The total number of days you owned the property is calculated using the contract purchase and sale dates, not settlement dates. You can also use the [Capital gains tax property exemption tool](https://www.ato.gov.au/calculators-and-tools/capital-gains-tax-property-exemption-tool) to work out what percentage of your capital gain is exempt from CGT. ### Example: rental property becomes your home Farnaz entered into a contract to purchase a property on 21 October 2019 for $449,000. She immediately rented out the property. The property was rented for 2 years, until Farnaz moved into the property on 16 November 2021. Farnaz lived in the property as her main residence until she signed a contract to sell her home on 1 April 2026 for $987,500. Farnaz works out her net capital gain as follows: 1. Capital gain is $538,500 (worked out as $987,500 − $449,000) 2. Number of days owned is 2,355 (21 October 2019 to 1 April 2026) 3. Number of days the property was used to produce assessable income is 757 (21 October 2019 to 15 November 2021) 4. Assessable capital gain is $538,500 × (757 ÷ 2,355) = $173,097 5. Net capital gain after applying the 50% CGT discount for owning the property for over 12 months is $86,548 (worked out as $173,097 × 50%) Farnaz includes a net capital gain of $86,548 in her 2026 tax return. correctness.justification: All rules, sections and methodology match the reference (s 118-192 reset to $420,000; $30,000 under s 110-25(5) and $20,000 under s 110-25(3); $470,000 cost base; $530,000 gain; s 118-185(2) day apportionment over the deemed ownership period), but both stated results diverge from the reference: the headline $176,667 uses a non-statutory 1/3 simplification, and the 'exact-day' figure uses 366 non-main-residence days against the reference's 365, producing $176,828 instead of $176,345 — a minor figure imprecision (the leap-year point is arguable, but graded against the reference the day count is wrong), and CGT event A1/s 104-10 is not identified.

completeness.justification: Covers every limb of the reference: the s 118-192 reset and disregard of pre-2020 expenditure, the s 118-145(4) point explaining why the six-year absence rule cannot help (a useful addition), both cost-base elements with a workings table, the s 118-185(2) formula, the deemed-ownership-period denominator, and extra caveats ($550,000 irrelevance; s 110-45(2) adjustment for capital-works deductions). The only omissions are express identification of CGT event A1 under s 104-10 and a day count reconciled to the reference's 365/1097.

faithfulness.justification: Effectively every load-bearing claim is anchored inline and verified from captured text: s 118-192(2) deemed acquisition at market value [[1]], s 118-145(4) mutual exclusivity [[2]], s 110-25(5) fourth element and s 110-25(3) second element [[3]], s 110-35(2) agent remuneration [[4]], the s 118-185(2) formula [[6]], and s 110-45(2) [[7]] are all present in the captures. It falls short of 5 only because the answer paraphrases the provisions rather than setting the operative statutory words out verbatim (though the full words sit in the captures), and the $550,000-irrelevance claim rests partly on secondary ATO guidance [[5]].

helpfulness.justification: Well-structured with a workings table, formula, and useful professional caveats (s 110-45 adjustment; irrelevance of the $550,000 value), but the headline bolds the simplified 1/3 figure as 'the' answer — a skimming practitioner takes away the wrong number — and there is no concrete closing next step (e.g. confirm the move-in date for the day count, or read TD 92/134 on apportionment), which level 3's working elements require.

citation_grounding.justification: Seven sources, six being the legislation itself with full operative text captured (ss 118-192, 118-145, 110-25, 110-35, 110-45, 118-185), each anchored at the specific claim it supports — including multi-source grounding of the agent-fees point (ss 110-25(3) and 110-35(2)) — and one ATO guidance page [[5]] used appropriately for a practice point whose statutory basis is separately grounded in s 118-185 [[6]]. No irrelevant, unanchored or unsupportive citations; every captured extract contains the pinpointed provision.

judge_output.summary: Correct method and sections throughout (s 118-192 reset, $470,000 cost base, $530,000 gain, s 118-185(2) apportionment) with exemplary claim-anchored primary citations, but the final figures ($176,667 headline; $176,828 exact-day) do not match the reference's $176,345 (365/1097).
